challenges.headline: 'Edit' framed as simple unlock
challenges.premise: The request describes managers editing and re-approving a signed document as if it were a single, direct action on the existing content.
challenges.alternative: The platform's own model treats an approved/signed version as frozen — any real change is a new version, with the old one retained and referenceable, and prior signatures invalidated or re-collected.
challenges.consequence: Building 'edit' as an in-place mutation would silently break signature defensibility and leave the audit trail incomplete — exactly the failure mode the platform is designed to prevent.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client upfront that this is a versioned supersession flow, not an in-place edit, and scope estimates accordingly.

challenges.headline: Undefined scope of 'managers'
challenges.premise: Any manager is implicitly assumed able to trigger an edit and re-approval on a signed document.
challenges.alternative: Given the legal weight of a signature, many organizations restrict who may reopen a signed document to the original approver, a compliance role, or a classification-specific circuit — not any manager.
challenges.consequence: An overly broad permission model lets unauthorized users alter legally binding content, undermining the very signature integrity the audit trail is meant to protect.
challenges.recommendation: Define precisely who can trigger a re-approval and whether the new approval circuit must mirror or can differ from the original signatories, before building permissions.

challenges.headline: Ambiguous 'current' during re-approval
challenges.premise: The request assumes the transition from signed-and-published to edited-and-pending is straightforward.
challenges.alternative: The platform explicitly separates the approval lifecycle from the publication lifecycle — a document can be approved but not yet published, or published then superseded. Which version people should act on while a re-approval is pending needs an explicit state.
challenges.consequence: Without a defined interim state, end users risk acting on a stale or since-superseded version while the new one is still in review.
challenges.recommendation: Define an explicit state machine for the pending-re-approval window before implementation — including what stays visible/downloadable and to whom.

challenges.headline: "Edit" implies in-place change
challenges.premise: The request is framed as editing the signed document directly.
challenges.alternative: The platform's own invariant treats a signed version as frozen — any change is a new Version, with the old one retained and stamped superseded, never a patch to the same record.
challenges.consequence: Building this as an in-place edit invalidates prior signatures silently, breaks the audit trail, and contradicts the platform's core Document/Version model — a much more expensive fix once built the wrong way.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client that this is supersession-based versioning, not a field-level edit, before any data-model work starts.

challenges.headline: Full circuit restart assumed
challenges.premise: Re-approval is treated as a single, undifferentiated event that presumably re-runs the whole original signing circuit.
challenges.alternative: Most document platforms distinguish a minor correction (typo, formatting) from a material change (terms, obligations) and route them through lighter vs. full circuits respectively.
challenges.consequence: Forcing every signatory to resign for a trivial fix creates friction and delay; but silently skipping signatories for a material change undermines the document's legal defensibility.
challenges.recommendation: Define change-severity tiers with the client and legal/compliance stakeholders before scoping the workflow.

challenges.headline: Managers act unilaterally
challenges.premise: Managers alone are named as the actor who can edit and invalidate a signed document's approval state.
challenges.alternative: Given the platform's approval-circuit pattern, original signatories or a records/compliance officer typically need visibility into, or consent for, an action that invalidates their own signature.
challenges.consequence: If managers can silently supersede a document others signed, signatories may contest the resigned version's validity later, and compliance officers lose the oversight the audit trail is meant to guarantee.
challenges.recommendation: Clarify whether original signatories must be notified or must consent before their signature is invalidated.
